newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico railroad turf battles seen fierce - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico railroad turf battles seen fierce - analysts.

text.p: Two railways that run north and south on either side of Mexico are likely to enter a bitter battle for cargo, but analysts say both lines will have to cooperate if they want to prosper.

The most coveted line, the Northeast, runs 4,282 kilometers (2,676 miles) up Mexico's eastern flank to the Texas crossing of Laredo and is due to start up private operations in a month's time after its selloff in December.
Against it stands the mammoth Pacific-North railroad, almost twice as long, but which analysts say has a poorer quality track.

It could get a major boost, however, if sole bidding group of miner Grupo Mexico SA, builder Empresas ICA Sociedad Controladora SA de CV and Union Pacific Corp won the rights to the rail in July, because analysts say Union Pacific has the pull to win cargo away from Laredo to its own Texas hub at Eagle Pass.

"If Union Pacific wanted to diversify traffic from the Northwest line to the Pacific-North, it most likely would be able to do so given its market clout above the border," Salomon Brothers analyst James J. Valentine said.
The potential railroad turf war already has analysts talking about competition in Mexican railroad traffic, expected to grow as privatization improves operations.
In December a venture between Transportacion Maritima Mexicana SA de CV (TMM) and Kansas City Southern Industries Inc, known as TFM, won the Northeast railroad.
"Union Pacific has more capital and resolve, a lower cost structure," Valentine said.

TFM paid a whopping $1.4 billion for the Northeast railroad, almost three times the bid of the second closest bidder. Even with the cost of improving the Pacific-North track, the winning bidder is likely to spend less money for the railroad, analysts said.
And Union Pacific has already planned a full-front attack on the Northeast's Laredo border crossing point, where about 80 percent of cargo into Mexico currently travels.
Officials have told analysts that if it won the railroad concession, it would aim to take over as much as 70 percent of cross-border traffic from the Laredo border entry.
Union Pacific's Mexico director general Juan Manuel Carreon said the Pacific-North connects with four Union Pacific routes north of the border and offers key synergies for the railroad.

Competition for cargo could be stiff, as the two railways service many of the same cities, such as key urban centers Mexico City and Monterrey. Yet analysts predict the lines would have to cooperate and allow each other trackage rights.

The Pacific-North provides only secondary access to Mexico City and would have to connect with the Northeast for more direct transport. Likewise, only the Pacific-North reaches Manzanillo port, which is operated by TMM.

"It seems logical that they will have to work with one another," Bear Stearns analyst Santiago Pique said. "Given the Pacific-North does not have direct access to Mexico City, (the line's winners) could get trackage rights on the Northeast."
"If Union Pacific wins the line, I think they and Kansas City Southern will happily co-exist to improve service for all customers," Salomon Brothers' Valentine said.
He added that Union Pacific has said it wants to hold only a 10 to 15 percent stake in the rail, while retaining management rights.
